did_you_know.text: Did you know? Isaiah opens the chapter with a personal declaration of thanks to the Lord for doing wondrous things and faithfully fulfilling his ancient plans.
Did you know? The Lord’s judgment is portrayed in the destruction of a fortified city and a foreign palace, until the city becomes a ruin and the palace is never rebuilt.

Did you know? Alongside judgment on the wicked, the Lord is described as a shelter and stronghold for the poor and needy in times of trouble, protecting them from the storm, the heat, and the pressure of tyrants.
Did you know? The vision of redemption includes a feast that the Lord prepares for all peoples on the mountain—a rich feast of fine food and well-aged wines.
Did you know? The chapter uses images of a covering and a veil spread over the nations; removing them symbolizes revealing what has been hidden from the world.
Did you know? One of the chapter’s central promises of redemption is that death will be swallowed up forever, the Lord will wipe away the tears, and he will remove the disgrace of his people.
Did you know? The people respond to the Lord’s salvation with joyful praise: they put their hope in him, and he saved them; therefore they rejoice and celebrate in his salvation.
Did you know? Moab is portrayed like straw trampled in water and mud, an image that illustrates its humiliation under the Lord’s hand.
Did you know? Moab’s humiliation also includes its pride: its attempt to spread out its hands cannot save it, and its pride is brought low along with its schemes.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Moab’s fortresses and walls are brought down to the ground and into the dust, emphasizing that human strength and pride cannot withstand the Lord’s judgment.
